record.original_question: Which is the coarsest relation such that, for every terminating rewrite relation, the union of that relation with the coarser relation preserves termination and remains fully invariant under instantiation? Without full invariance, is encompassment the coarsest relation that preserves termination?

evidence.quote: Which is the coarsest relation such that its union with any rewrite relation preserves termination?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Work in the setting of first-order term rewriting over a fixed signature, with terms built from function symbols and a countable set of variables. A binary relation $\to$ on terms is called a rewrite relation if it is closed under contexts and under substitutions; it is fully invariant (under instantiation) if $s \to t$ implies $\sigma(s) \to \sigma(t)$ for every substitution $\sigma$. A rewrite relation $\to$ is terminating if there is no infinite chain $t_0 \to t_1 \to t_2 \to \cdots$.

The encompassment relation $\unrhd_\sigma$ is defined by: $s \unrhd_\sigma t$ iff some subterm of $s$ is an instance of $t$ (equivalently, $t$ matches a subterm of $s$). 

Determine the coarsest binary relation $R$ on terms such that, for every terminating rewrite relation $\to$, the union $\to \cup\, R$ is terminating and remains fully invariant under instantiation.

Moreover, if the requirement of full invariance is dropped, decide whether the encompassment relation $\unrhd_\sigma$ is the coarsest relation $R$ such that $\to \cup\, R$ is terminating whenever $\to$ is a terminating rewrite relation.
artifact.status_search_result: The question appears as one of the listed open problems in rewriting (Dershowitz-style problem collections), with the encompassment relation being a conjectured candidate. No published proof or refutation of either part was found in available sources, so it is treated as open.
